Lesson A0-04: Greeting and Basic Politeness ​

Level: A0 (Foundations)
CEFR Level: A0
Duration: 75 minutes
New Vocabulary: 40 words
Grammar Focus: Time-of-day greetings; politeness formulas (formal and informal); "Hoe gaat het?" structure; leave-taking expressions; simple imperatives for politeness

Lesson Goal ​

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to greet people appropriately for different times of day, ask how someone is and respond naturally, use politeness words correctly (choosing formal or informal), and say goodbye using various leave-taking expressions.

Previous Knowledge ​

You must have completed A0-01: Understanding Sounds, A0-02: Introducing Yourself, and A0-03: Describing People and Family before starting this lesson.

From A0-01, A0-02, and A0-03, you should know:

  • Dutch pronunciation and alphabet
  • Personal pronouns (ik, jij, hij, zij, het, u, wij, jullie, zij)
  • Present tense of "zijn" (ben, bent, is, zijn)
  • Present tense of "hebben" (heb, hebt, heeft, hebben)
  • de/het articles and basic word order
  • Demonstratives (deze, dit, die, dat)
  • Basic adjectives (oud, jong, aardig, groot, klein, goed, blij)
  • Simple yes/no questions with inversion

This lesson focuses on social protocols and formulaic language used in greeting and politeness contexts.

Why This Matters ​

Every conversation starts with a greeting. Learning how to greet people appropriately for the time of day, ask how they are, and respond politely is one of the most practical skills in any language. In Dutch culture, where greetings and politeness work differently than in English, getting these right shows respect and cultural awareness. This lesson teaches you the safe, natural phrases that make you sound competent and socially aware from the very first interaction.

Grammar ​

This lesson introduces six core grammar concepts for greeting, politeness, and social interaction:

1. Greetings by Time of Day ​

Explanation

Dutch has neutral greetings that work anytime (hallo, dag) and time-specific greetings:

  • Goedemorgen (good morning) -- used before noon
  • Goedemiddag (good afternoon) -- used after noon, typically afternoon
  • Goedenavond (good evening) -- used in the evening
  • Goedendag (good day) -- formal alternative to hallo; works all day
  • Welterusten (sleep well) -- only for bedtime/nighttime parting, not a greeting

Why it matters: Using the correct time-of-day greeting shows awareness and respect. It's a key way to make a good first impression in Dutch society.

Examples:

DutchEnglish
Goedemorgen, ik ben Anna.Good morning, I am Anna.
Goedemiddag, meneer.Good afternoon, sir.
Goedenavond, mevrouw.Good evening, madam.
Hallo, ik ben Mete.Hello, I am Mete.
Dag, tot ziens.Hello/Bye, see you.

Common mistakes:

  • ❌ Goedenacht as a greeting → ✅ Welterusten (for bedtime only; goedenacht is archaic)
  • ❌ Hallo used too formally → ✅ Goedemiddag (hallo is fine, but time-of-day greetings are more polished)
  • ❌ Using dag only for goodbye → ✅ Dag can mean hello or goodbye (context determines meaning)

Contrast with A0-02/A0-03:

A0-02 and A0-03 focused on introducing yourself. A0-04 adds the social wrapper: how to start that introduction appropriately for the time of day.

2. Basic Politeness Formulas ​

Explanation

Dutch has core politeness words, with formal and informal variants:

ContextInformalFormal
Please/here you arealsjeblieftalstublieft
Thank youdank jedank u
Thank you (emphatic)dankjeweldankuwel
Thank you (standard)bedanktbedankt
You're welcomegeen dank / graag gedaangeen dank / graag gedaan
Sorry / Excuse mesorry / pardonpardon / excuseer

Why it matters: Using the right level of formality (je vs u) shows cultural awareness. Formal politeness with a stranger or authority figure is respectful; informal with a friend is natural.

Examples:

DutchEnglish
Dank je, Emma.Thank you, Emma. (informal)
Dank u, meneer.Thank you, sir. (formal)
Alsjeblieft.Please / Here you go. (informal)
Alstublieft.Please / Here you are. (formal)
Sorry.Sorry.
Geen dank.You're welcome / No thanks needed.

Common mistakes:

  • ❌ Overusing alsjeblieft/alstublieft → ✅ Dutch uses fewer "please" equivalents than English (tone and context carry politeness instead)
  • ❌ Using dank je with strangers → ✅ Use dank u with people you don't know well
  • ❌ Saying vaarwel for goodbye → ✅ Vaarwel is rare/archaic; use tot ziens

Contrast with A0-02/A0-03:

A0-02 introduced pronouns (jij/je vs u). A0-04 shows these distinctions in real politeness choices.

3. "Hoe Gaat Het Met Je/U?" Structure ​

Explanation

The most natural A0 "How are you?" pattern is "Hoe gaat het?" (literally "How goes it?"), optionally with "met + pronoun":

StructureFormalityExample
Hoe gaat het?NeutralHoe gaat het?
Hoe gaat het met je?InformalHoe gaat het met je?
Hoe gaat het met u?FormalHoe gaat het met u?
Hoe gaat het met jou?EmphaticHoe gaat het met jou? (And you?)

Why it matters: This structure opens a greeting into a real conversation. It shows interest and creates a social bond.

Examples:

DutchEnglish
Hoe gaat het?How are you?
Hoe gaat het met je?How are you? (informal)
Hoe gaat het met u?How are you? (formal)
Goed, dank je. En met jou?Good, thanks. And you?
Met mij gaat het goed.I am doing well.

Common mistakes:

  • ❌ Hoe ben je? as a direct translation → ✅ Hoe gaat het? (The Dutch structure is different)
  • ❌ Hoe gaat het jij? → ✅ Hoe gaat het met je? (Need "met")
  • ❌ Using jij where je sounds more natural → ✅ Hoe gaat het met je? (je is often preferred in speech)

Contrast with A0-02/A0-03:

A0-02 and A0-03 used "zijn" and "hebben" for self-introduction and description. A0-04 uses "gaat" (goes) as an idiomatic Dutch way to ask about state of being.

4. Present Tense of "Zijn" in Greeting Responses ​

Explanation

Learners can respond to "Hoe gaat het?" in two ways:

Direct response (most natural):

  • Het gaat goed. (It's going well.)
  • Met mij gaat het goed. (I'm doing well.)

Adjective response (also natural, but be careful):

  • Ik ben blij. (I am happy.)
  • Ik ben goed. (I am good—but this means "morally good," not "I'm well," so avoid)

Why it matters: Knowing which response sounds natural keeps your reply grammatical and appropriate.

Examples:

DutchEnglish
Het gaat goed.It is going well.
Met mij gaat het goed.I am doing well.
Ik ben blij.I am happy.
Ik ben oké.I am okay.
Heel goed, dank je.Very well, thanks.

Common mistakes:

  • ❌ Ik ben goed → ✅ Het gaat goed (Ik ben goed sounds like "I am morally good," not "I'm well")
  • ❌ Responding with only "goed" → ✅ Add "dank je" or "dank u" (Full responses are more natural: "Goed, dank je.")
  • ❌ Ik heb goed → ✅ Het gaat goed (gaat, not hebben)

Contrast with A0-02/A0-03:

A0-02 and A0-03 used "zijn" for identity (Ik ben Anna) and description (De opa is oud). A0-04 uses "gaat" as the idiomatic verb for "How are you?" responses.

5. Leave-Taking Expressions ​

Explanation

Dutch has several ways to say goodbye, some neutral and some with time expectations:

ExpressionMeaningUse
Tot ziensGoodbye / See youStandard, polite goodbye
Tot straksSee you soon / later todayWhen you'll see them again soon
Tot morgenSee you tomorrowWhen you'll meet the next day
Tot laterSee you laterInformal, when you'll see them later
Tot snelSee you soonQuick goodbye, informal
DoeiByeInformal, friendly
DagByeNeutral, can be hello or goodbye
CiaoByeInformal, borrowed from Italian
LaterLater / See yaVery informal, slang

Why it matters: Choosing the right goodbye shows you understand social context and have closure skills.

Examples:

DutchEnglish
Tot ziens.Goodbye / See you.
Tot straks.See you soon / later today.
Tot morgen.See you tomorrow.
Doei!Bye!
Tot ziens, dank u.Goodbye, thank you.

Common mistakes:

  • ❌ Using vaarwel → ✅ Tot ziens (Vaarwel is archaic/formal)
  • ❌ Tot ziens with someone you'll see in 5 minutes → ✅ Tot straks (Be specific about timing)
  • ❌ Doei in a formal context → ✅ Tot ziens (Tot ziens is safer in formal situations)

Contrast with A0-02/A0-03:

A0-02 and A0-03 did not focus on closing interactions. A0-04 adds social closure and time management ("when will we see each other again?").

6. Simple Imperative Forms for Polite Interaction ​

Explanation

The Dutch imperative uses the bare verb stem:

  • Zeg (say) → Zeg hallo. (Say hello.)
  • Vraag (ask) → Vraag hoe gaat het. (Ask how are you.)
  • Doe (do) → Doe rustig. (Take it easy.)
  • Wacht (wait) → Wacht even. (Wait a moment.)
  • Kom (come) → Kom binnen. (Come in.)

For formal "u," add -t: Komt u binnen (Please come in, formal).

Why it matters: A0 classroom instructions often use imperatives: "Zeg hallo," "Vraag je partner," etc. Learning these keeps learners responsive.

Examples:

DutchEnglish
Zeg hallo.Say hello.
Vraag: Hoe gaat het?Ask: How are you?
Doe even rustig.Take it easy / Be calm.
Wacht even, alsjeblieft.Wait a moment, please.
Komt u binnen.Please come in. (formal)

Common mistakes:

  • ❌ Zegt hallo (to jij) → ✅ Zeg hallo (Don't add -t for informal)
  • ❌ Using infinitive in imperative → ✅ Zeg, not zeggen (Use bare stem)
  • ❌ Kom hier, alsjeblieft → ✅ Kom hier, alsjeblieft (Correct; "alsjeblieft" softens the command)

Contrast with A0-02/A0-03:

A0-02 and A0-03 did not focus on commands. A0-04 introduces imperatives as a classroom and social tool for giving polite instructions.

Grammar Reasoning ​

Why Time-of-Day Greetings Matter ​

English has one greeting ("Hello") for all times. Dutch requires awareness of time. This might feel extra work initially, but it trains you to be culturally attuned. Dutch culture values punctuality and context awareness; time-appropriate greetings reflect that.

Why "Gaat" Not "Ben" for "How Are You?" ​

English uses "to be" (How are you?), but Dutch idiomatic says "How does it go?" (Hoe gaat het?). This is a different cultural metaphor: Dutch asks about motion/progress ("how is it going?"), not identity. Learning this pattern now prevents fossilized errors later.

Why Politeness Has Formal and Informal Variants ​

Many European languages distinguish formal and informal address. Dutch does this with u vs jij/je. Using the wrong level can sound rude or overly stiff. A0 learners need to see this distinction in action, not just in pronouns.

Why Dutch Uses Fewer "Please/Thank You" Than English ​

English speakers often soften every request with "please" and every acceptance with "thank you." Dutch relies more on tone, efficiency, directness, and context. Over-thanking in Dutch can sound insincere or overly formal. A0 learners should understand this cultural difference.

Why Imperatives Are A0 Grammar ​

Classroom instructions require imperatives: "Zeg hallo," "Vraag je partner," "Luister." Teaching imperatives early makes the classroom functional.

Pronunciation ​

Greetings and politeness words have predictable pronunciation once you know Dutch vowel sounds from A0-01.

Time-of-Day Greetings ​

  • goedemorgen (GHOO-duh-MOR-ghun) -- Two syllables run together, then "morning" stress
  • goedemiddag (GHOO-duh-MID-dakh) -- Similar pattern, "afternoon" stress
  • goedenavond (GHOO-duhn-AH-vont) -- "evening" stress on second "a"
  • hallo (HAH-loh) -- First syllable stressed
  • goedendag (GHOO-duhn-DAKH) -- "day" is final stress
  • welterusten (vel-tuh-RUS-tun) -- Stress on first long vowel, then relax

Politeness Words ​

  • alstublieft (ahl-stu-BLEEFT) -- Three syllables, stress on last
  • alsjeblieft (ahl-shuh-BLEEFT) -- Same pattern, informal
  • dank (DAHNK) -- Short a, nasal ending
  • dankjewel (DAHNK-yuh-VEL) -- Three syllables, stress on first
  • sorry (SOR-ee) -- Two syllables, first stressed
  • pardon (par-DON) -- Stress on second syllable
  • excuseer (eks-koo-ZEER) -- Stress on last syllable
  • graag gedaan (GHRAAKH khuh-DAHN) -- Two words, first stressed

Leave-Taking Expressions ​

  • tot ziens (tot ZEENS) -- Two words, second is long i sound
  • tot straks (tot STRAHKS) -- Two words, second stressed
  • tot morgen (tot MOR-ghun) -- Second word stressed
  • doei (DOO-ee) -- Long o + long i, friendly tone
  • ciao (CHOW) -- Italian borrowed word, like English "ciao"
  • dag (DAKH) -- Short a, crisscross sound

Response Phrases ​

  • goed (KHOOT) -- Long o + d
  • heel goed (HAYL KHOOT) -- Two words, first has long a
  • prima (PREE-mah) -- Two syllables, first stressed
  • niet slecht (neet SLEKHT) -- Short i + sh-kh ending
  • oké (oh-KAY) -- Two syllables, second stressed

Dialogue ​

Here are five realistic dialogues showing greeting, politeness, and leave-taking in different contexts.

Dialogue 1: Morning Greeting — Informal ​

Dutch:

A: Goedemorgen, Emma. Hoe gaat het?
B: Goed, dank je. En met jou?
A: Ook goed. Tot straks!
B: Doei!

Translation:

A: Good morning, Emma. How are you?
B: Good, thanks. And you?
A: Good too. See you soon!
B: Bye!

Dialogue 2: Afternoon Greeting — Formal ​

Dutch:

A: Goedemiddag, mevrouw. Hoe gaat het met u?
B: Prima, dank u. En met u?
A: Met mij gaat het goed. Alstublieft.
B: Dankuwel. Tot ziens.

Translation:

A: Good afternoon, madam. How are you?
B: Fine, thank you. And you?
A: I am well. Here you are.
B: Thank you. Goodbye.

Dialogue 3: Evening Greeting ​

Dutch:

A: Goedenavond, meneer.
B: Goedenavond. Hoe gaat het?
A: Niet slecht, dank u.
B: Prima. Tot ziens.

Translation:

A: Good evening, sir.
B: Good evening. How are you?
A: Not bad, thank you.
B: Fine. Goodbye.

Dialogue 4: Politeness in a Small Interaction ​

Dutch:

A: Pardon.
B: Ja?
A: Sorry. Vraag: hoe gaat het?
B: Goed, dank je. Geen dank.

Translation:

A: Excuse me.
B: Yes?
A: Sorry. Ask: how are you?
B: Good, thanks. You're welcome.

Dialogue 5: Formal vs Informal Contrast ​

Dutch (Informal):

A: Hallo, ik ben Tom.
B: Hallo Tom, ik ben Sara. Hoe gaat het met je?
A: Goed, dank je.

Dutch (Formal):

C: Goedendag, meneer. Hoe gaat het met u?
D: Prima, dank u. Tot ziens.

Translation (Informal):

A: Hello, I am Tom.
B: Hello Tom, I am Sara. How are you?
A: Good, thanks.

Translation (Formal):

C: Good day, sir. How are you?
D: Fine, thank you. Goodbye.

Reading ​

Read this short text about a greeting exchange. It uses only grammar and vocabulary you've learned in A0-01, A0-02, A0-03, and A0-04.

Dutch Text:

Goedemorgen. Ik ben Anna. Hoe gaat het met je?

Met mij gaat het goed, dank je. Ik ben blij. Jij bent vriendelijk. Dank je.

Graag gedaan. Tot later.

Doei!

English Translation:

Good morning. I am Anna. How are you?

I am doing well, thanks. I am happy. You are friendly. Thank you.

You're welcome. See you later.

Bye!

Listening ​

Listen to these short greeting exchanges. You can read the transcripts below. Try to understand as much as you can before reading the translations.

Conversation 1: Informal Morning Greeting

[Audio would be located at /shared/assets/audio/A0-04-listening-01.mp3]

Transcript:

A: Goedemorgen, Jan!
B: Goedemorgen, Emma. Hoe gaat het?
A: Heel goed, dank je. En met jou?
B: Prima. Tot straks!
A: Doei!

Translation:

A: Good morning, Jan!
B: Good morning, Emma. How are you?
A: Very well, thanks. And you?
B: Fine. See you later!
A: Bye!

Comprehension Questions:

  1. Hoe gaat het met Emma? (How is Emma?)
    Answer: Heel goed (Very well)

  2. Wanneer zien ze elkaar weer? (When will they see each other again?)
    Answer: Straks (Soon / Later today)

Conversation 2: Formal Afternoon Greeting

[Audio would be located at /shared/assets/audio/A0-04-listening-02.mp3]

Transcript:

A: Goedemiddag, mevrouw.
B: Goedemiddag, meneer.
A: Hoe gaat het met u?
B: Goed, dank u. Alstublieft.
A: Dankuwel. Tot ziens.

Translation:

A: Good afternoon, madam.
B: Good afternoon, sir.
A: How are you?
B: Good, thank you. Here you are.
A: Thank you. Goodbye.

Comprehension Questions:

  1. Is dit een formeel of informeel gesprek? (Is this a formal or informal conversation?)
    Answer: Formeel (Formal)

  2. Wat zeggen ze aan het einde? (What do they say at the end?)
    Answer: Tot ziens (Goodbye)

Speaking ​

Practice greeting people appropriately for different times of day and contexts.

Exercise 1: Time-Based Greetings ​

Scenario: You're greeting someone at different times.

Morning (09:00): Goedemorgen. Hoe gaat het?

Afternoon (14:00): Goedemiddag. Hoe gaat het met je?

Evening (19:00): Goedenavond. Hoe gaat het?

Exercise 2: Formal Greeting Exchange ​

Scenario: You're meeting a teacher or boss.

What you say:

  1. Greet them appropriately for the time.
  2. Ask how they are using formal "u."
  3. Respond to their question about you.
  4. Thank them and say goodbye.

Model Response:

"Goedemiddag, mevrouw. Hoe gaat het met u? Met mij gaat het goed, dank u. Dank u. Tot ziens."

Exercise 3: Informal Greeting with a Classmate ​

Scenario: You meet a classmate.

What you say:

  1. Greet them informally.
  2. Ask how they are.
  3. Respond to their question.
  4. Say goodbye using an informal expression.

Model Response:

"Hallo, Jan. Hoe gaat het met je? Prima, dank je. Tot straks!"

Exercise 4: Complete Greeting Dialogue ​

Scenario: Role-play a greeting exchange with a partner.

Partner A: Start the conversation (morning greeting + how are you).
Partner B: Respond (answer + how are you back).
Partner A: Respond to them (answer + goodbye).
Partner B: Respond (goodbye).

Writing ​

Exercise 1: Fill in the Blanks — Greetings and Politeness ​

Complete each sentence with the correct greeting, politeness word, or leave-taking expression.

  1. ___ gaat het? (How) → Hoe
  2. Het gaat ___. (well) → goed
  3. ___ je, Emma. (Thank you informal) → Dank
  4. ___ u, meneer. (Please formal) → Alstublieft
  5. Tot ___. (goodbye) → ziens
  6. ___ straks! (See you soon) → Tot
  7. ___, ik ben Anna. (Good morning) → Goedemorgen
  8. Met mij gaat het ___. (good) → goed
  9. ___, Emma! (Bye informal) → Doei
  10. ___ je, Jan. (Thank you informal emphatic) → Dankjewel

Answers: 1. Hoe 2. goed 3. Dank 4. Alstublieft 5. ziens 6. Tot 7. Goedemorgen 8. goed 9. Doei 10. Dankjewel

Exercise 2: Formal vs Informal Selection ​

Choose the correct word for each context.

  1. Talking to your teacher: dank je / dank u → dank u
  2. Talking to your classmate: Hoe gaat het met je / u? → met je
  3. Saying please to a shopkeeper: alsjeblieft / alstublieft → alstublieft
  4. Saying goodbye to a friend: Tot ziens / Doei → Doei (or Tot ziens is fine too)
  5. Greeting at 14:00: Goedemorgen / Goedemiddag → Goedemiddag

Exercise 3: Write a Greeting Dialogue ​

Write a short dialogue (4-6 lines) between two people greeting each other. Include:

  • One time-of-day greeting
  • One "Hoe gaat het?" question
  • One response with "Het gaat goed" or similar
  • One politeness word (dank je or alsjeblieft)
  • One leave-taking expression

Model Answer:

A: Goedemorgen, Emma!
B: Goedemorgen. Hoe gaat het met je?
A: Prima, dank je. En met jou?
B: Goed. Tot straks, alsjeblieft?
A: Tot straks!

Exercise 4: Time-of-Day Appropriate Responses ​

Complete each response appropriately for the time of day.

  1. (09:00) A: Goedemorgen! B: ___. → Goedemorgen. Hoe gaat het?
  2. (14:00) A: Goedemiddag, mevrouw. B: ___. → Goedemiddag. Prima, dank u.
  3. (19:00) A: Goedenavond. B: ___. → Goedenavond. Met mij gaat het goed.
  4. (All times) A: Hoe gaat het? B: ___. → Goed, dank je. En met jou?

Common Mistakes ​

Mistake 1: Using the Wrong Time-of-Day Greeting ​

Wrong: Goedemorgen at 14:00 / Goedemiddag at 08:00
Right: Goedemiddag at 14:00 / Goedemorgen at 08:00
Why: Time-of-day greetings must match the actual time. Using the wrong one sounds unaware or confused.

Mistake 2: Not Using "Met" in "Hoe Gaat Het?" ​

Wrong: Hoe gaat het je?
Right: Hoe gaat het met je?
Why: The structure requires "met" (with).

Mistake 3: Using "Hoe Ben Je?" Instead of "Hoe Gaat Het?" ​

Wrong: Hoe ben je? (This is ungrammatical or means "How are you literally made?")
Right: Hoe gaat het? (This is the natural Dutch "How are you?")
Why: Dutch idiom uses "gaat" (goes), not "ben" (is).

Mistake 4: Saying "Ik Ben Goed" for "I'm Well" ​

Wrong: Ik ben goed. (This sounds like "I am morally good.")
Right: Het gaat goed. / Het gaat goed met mij. / Heel goed, dank je.
Why: "Ik ben goed" misses the intended meaning.

Mistake 5: Confusing Informal and Formal Politeness Words ​

Wrong: Dank u with a classmate / Dank je with a teacher
Right: Dank je with classmates / Dank u with teachers and strangers
Why: Register matters in Dutch. Using the wrong one can sound rude or overly formal.

Mistake 6: Overusing "Alsjeblieft/Alstublieft" ​

Wrong: Alsjeblieft, can you help me? (repeating "please" constantly)
Right: Can you help me? (Trust tone and context to convey politeness)
Why: Dutch uses "please" less often than English. Over-using it sounds insincere or foreign.

Mistake 7: Using "Vaarwel" for Goodbye ​

Wrong: Vaarwel.
Right: Tot ziens / Doei / Tot straks
Why: Vaarwel is archaic and rarely used in modern Dutch.

Mistake 8: Not Adding "Dank Je/U" in Responses ​

Wrong: Heel goed.
Right: Heel goed, dank je.
Why: Adding thanks makes the response more complete and polite.

Dutch Insight ​

Greeting Customs in the Netherlands ​

Handshakes: In professional or first-meeting contexts, a firm handshake is standard, usually once.

Cheek kisses: Among friends, family, or social acquaintances, Dutch people often use three cheek kisses (the common sequence is right-left-right). This is called "drie zoenen" (three kisses) or "kussen" (kissing). It's not used in formal or first professional meetings.

Context determines the greeting: You'll shake hands in a job interview, use cheek kisses with friends at a party, and use a simple nod or "hallo" with a cashier.

Why Dutch Politeness Can Seem Abrupt ​

English speakers often soften requests and responses with "please" and "thank you." Dutch relies more on:

  • Clear, direct tone -- Dutch communication values efficiency and honesty
  • Context -- In a café, you order coffee without "please"; the setting and tone convey politeness
  • Minimal softeners -- "Dank je" is often enough; you don't need "Alsjeblieft, can you please..." in Dutch

This is not rudeness; it's a different communication style. Dutch culture values directness and respects your time.

Formal vs Informal Address (U vs Jij/Je) ​

Use "u" with:

  • Strangers
  • People older than you (by 10-20+ years)
  • Doctors, teachers, authority figures
  • First professional meetings
  • Formal service contexts (banks, government offices)

Use "jij" or "je" with:

  • Friends and family
  • Peers (classmates, coworkers your age)
  • Children
  • Many casual Dutch workplaces (Dutch culture is relatively informal)

When unsure: Start formal (use "u"). Dutch people will tell you if they prefer "jij," and it's not rude to ask: "Zeg maar je" (You can say "jij" to me).

Time-of-Day Context ​

  • Goedemorgen: Before noon, in shops, workplaces, schools
  • Goedemiddag: After noon, especially 12:00-17:00
  • Goedenavond: From evening onwards (roughly 17:00 or sunset)
  • Goedendag: Formal, works all day; used when exact time is unclear or in formal settings
  • Hallo/Dag: Work anytime; less formal than time-specific greetings

Regional and Generational Variation ​

  • Netherlands Dutch: Uses "tot ziens," "doei," "dag," "later"
  • Flemish (Belgian): May use "houdoe," "tot slot," or French-influenced "salut"
  • Younger Dutch speakers: More likely to use "doei," "later," "ciao" (informal)
  • Older or formal: More likely to use "tot ziens" (formal goodbye)

This lesson prioritizes Netherlands Dutch and informal contexts suitable for A0 learners.

Memory Tricks ​

Trick 1: Time-of-Day Greetings by Syllable Count ​

  • Goedemorgen (4 syllables) = morning (more syllables for early in day)
  • Goedemiddag (4 syllables) = afternoon (mid-day)
  • Goedenavond (4 syllables) = evening (longer word for longer daylight going away)

Not a perfect rule, but helps you remember which is which!

Trick 2: Je vs U = Informal vs Formal ​

JE = informal (J sounds like "friends" in some accents)
U = formal/respectful (U sounds like "you" in a respectful way)

When in doubt: Start with "u." If someone likes "jij," they'll say "Zeg maar je."

Trick 3: "Hoe Gaat Het?" = "How Goes It?" ​

Think of it like asking about the progress of someone's day/life:

Hoe gaat het? = How's it going? / How's the journey?

This is why "gaat" (goes), not "ben" (is).

Trick 4: Politeness Word Pairs ​

Please:

  • Informal = alsjeblieft (ahl-shuh-BLEEFT, sounds like "as-you-please" run together)
  • Formal = alstublieft (ahl-stu-BLEEFT, sounds like "as-you-please" more crisp)

Thank you:

  • Informal = dank je (thank you) or dankjewel (thank you! emphatic)
  • Formal = dank u or dankuwel

Pattern: If it has a "j" sound (je), it's informal. If it has "u," it's formal.

Trick 5: Leave-Taking by Time Expectation ​

  • Tot ziens (see you) = Neutral, could be days/weeks
  • Tot straks (see you soon/later) = Same day, could be hours
  • Tot morgen (see you tomorrow) = Specific next day
  • Doei / Dag / Later = Informal, doesn't imply specific timing

Choose based on when you'll actually see them!

Active Recall ​

Do NOT look at the answers yet. Write or say your responses.

  1. What are the three time-of-day greetings in Dutch, and what times do they correspond to?

  2. How do you ask "How are you?" in Dutch in both formal and informal ways?

  3. What is the difference between "dank je" and "dank u"?

  4. Why do Dutch speakers use "Hoe gaat het?" instead of "Hoe ben je?" for "How are you?"

  5. Name at least three different ways to say goodbye in Dutch.

  6. When would you use "u" instead of "jij/je" in a greeting?

  7. Translate to Dutch: "Good morning, sir. How are you?"

  8. What is the correct way to ask "How are you?" if you want to add a pronoun for emphasis?

  9. Is it polite to respond with only "Goed" to "Hoe gaat het?", or should you add something else?

  10. What do you call the three cheek greeting in Dutch?

Answers:

  1. Three time-of-day greetings:

    • Goedemorgen (good morning) = before noon
    • Goedemiddag (good afternoon) = afternoon, typically 12:00-17:00
    • Goedenavond (good evening) = evening onwards

  2. How to ask "How are you?"

    • Informal: Hoe gaat het met je?
    • Formal: Hoe gaat het met u?
    • Neutral: Hoe gaat het? (works in most contexts)

  3. Difference between "dank je" and "dank u":

    • Dank je = informal (with friends, peers, family)
    • Dank u = formal (with strangers, authority figures, older people)

  4. Why "gaat" instead of "ben": Dutch idiom asks about progress/motion ("How goes it?"), not identity ("How are you?"). It's a cultural difference in how Dutch views the concept of "being well."

  5. Three ways to say goodbye:

    • Tot ziens (see you / goodbye)
    • Doei (bye, informal)
    • Tot morgen (see you tomorrow)
    • Other options: Tot straks, dag, later, ciao

  6. When to use "u": With strangers, people older than you, authority figures (teachers, doctors), first professional meetings, formal service contexts.

  7. "Good morning, sir. How are you?"Goedemorgen, meneer. Hoe gaat het met u? OR Goedemorgen, meneer. Hoe gaat het?

  8. How to ask with emphasis:Hoe gaat het met jou? (And you? with emphasis, literally "How goes it with you?")

  9. Responding with only "Goed": It's polite, but adding "dank je" or "dank u" is better: Goed, dank je. Full responses sound more complete.

  10. Three cheek greeting:Drie zoenen (three kisses) or just kussen (kissing).

Quiz ​

Read each question. Write or say your answer. Then check the Answer Key below.

Question 1: What time-of-day greeting would you use at 14:00 (2:00 PM)? ​

A) Goedemorgen
B) Goedemiddag
C) Goedenavond
D) Hallo

Correct Answer: B) Goedemiddag (14:00 is afternoon)

Question 2: How do you ask "How are you?" formally in Dutch? ​

A) Hoe ben je?
B) Hoe ben u?
C) Hoe gaat het met u?
D) Hoe gaat u?

Correct Answer: C) Hoe gaat het met u? (The natural Dutch structure uses "gaat")

Question 3: Which response to "Hoe gaat het?" is most natural? ​

A) Ik ben goed.
B) Het gaat goed.
C) Goed gaat het.
D) Goed ben ik.

Correct Answer: B) Het gaat goed. ("Ik ben goed" means "I am morally good," not "I'm well")

Question 4: What is the informal way to say "Thank you"? ​

A) Dank u
B) Dank je
C) Dankuwel
D) Bedankt

Correct Answer: B) Dank je (Use with friends and peers)

Question 5: When should you use "u" instead of "je/jij"? ​

A) Always
B) Never
C) With strangers, older people, and authority figures
D) Only at night

Correct Answer: C) With strangers, older people, and authority figures

Question 6: Which is the most formal goodbye? ​

A) Doei
B) Dag
C) Tot ziens
D) Later

Correct Answer: C) Tot ziens (Most polite and standard)

Question 7: What does "Hoe gaat het?" literally mean? ​

A) How are you?
B) How goes it?
C) How is it?
D) What is it?

Correct Answer: B) How goes it? (Dutch uses "goes" idiomatically for "How are you?")

Question 8: Which phrase is correct to add to a goodbye for "See you tomorrow"? ​

A) Tot vandaag
B) Tot morgen
C) Tot gisteren
D) Tot nu

Correct Answer: B) Tot morgen (Tomorrow)

Question 9: What would you add to "Goedemorgen" to make it more polite/complete? ​

A) Hoe heet je?
B) Hoe gaat het met je?
C) Dank je
D) Doei

Correct Answer: B) Hoe gaat het met je? (Adds engagement and turns greeting into conversation)

Question 10: Which of these is NOT a way to say goodbye in Dutch? ​

A) Tot ziens
B) Doei
C) Vaarwel
D) Tot morgen

Correct Answer: C) Vaarwel (This is archaic and rarely used in modern Dutch)

Question 11: How do you soften a command in Dutch (make it more polite)? ​

A) Add nothing; tone handles it
B) Add "alsjeblieft" or "alstublieft"
C) Add an imperative to the end
D) Repeat the command twice

Correct Answer: B) Add "alsjeblieft" or "alstublieft" (Example: "Kom hier, alsjeblieft.")

Question 12: What is the correct structure: "Hoe gaat het ___?" ​

A) jij
B) je
C) met je
D) met

Correct Answer: C) met je (Hoe gaat het met je?)

Question 13: Translate to Dutch: "Very well, thank you." ​

A) Goed, dank je.
B) Heel goed, dank je.
C) Prima goed, dank je.
D) Dank je, heel goed.

Correct Answer: B) Heel goed, dank je. (Emphasis on "very")

Question 14: If someone greets you with "u," how should you typically respond? ​

A) Use "jij" to be friendly
B) Use "u" back to match their formality
C) Use "je" to lighten the mood
D) Don't use a pronoun

Correct Answer: B) Use "u" back to match their formality (Mutual respect; they can later suggest "jij")

Question 15: Which word means "say" in the imperative form? ​

A) Zeggen
B) Zeg
C) Zei
D) Gezegd

Correct Answer: B) Zeg (Bare stem for imperative)

Homework ​

Do this after completing the lesson. Plan for 35-45 minutes.

Task 1: Time-Based Greetings ​

Write the correct greeting for each time:

  • 08:00 → ___
  • 13:00 → ___
  • 18:00 → ___
  • 22:00 (bedtime) → ___

Then practice saying each aloud 3 times.

Answers: 08:00 → Goedemorgen; 13:00 → Goedemiddag; 18:00 → Goedenavond; 22:00 → Welterusten

Task 2: Politeness Register Practice ​

Write sentences using the correct formal or informal politeness word for each context.

  1. Talking to your teacher: ___ (thank you)
  2. Talking to your friend: ___ (please)
  3. Talking to a shopkeeper: ___ (thank you)
  4. Talking to your classmate: ___ (here you go)

Task 3: Write Three Complete Greeting Exchanges ​

Write three short dialogues (3-4 lines each):

  1. Morning, informal: Between two classmates
  2. Afternoon, formal: Between a customer and a teacher
  3. Evening, casual: Between two friends saying goodbye

Requirements: Include time-of-day greeting, one "Hoe gaat het?" question, one response, and one leave-taking expression in each.

Task 4: Formal vs Informal Selection ​

Read each scenario and choose the correct form:

  1. Greeting your best friend: Hoe gaat het met je / u?
  2. Greeting your boss: Hoe gaat het met je / u?
  3. Saying thanks to a classmate: Dank je / u
  4. Saying please to a waiter: Alsjeblieft / Alstublieft
  5. Saying goodbye to a stranger: Doei / Tot ziens

Task 5: Pronunciation Practice ​

Choose one greeting and one politeness formula. Say them aloud 5 times each, focusing on stress and vowel sounds:

  • Greeting: Goedemorgen / Goedemiddag / Goedenavond
  • Politeness: Alstublieft / Dank u / Tot ziens

Record yourself if possible.

Task 6: Write Your Own Dialogue ​

Write a greeting dialogue you might have with someone in Dutch (a classmate, teacher, or friend). Include:

  • Appropriate time-of-day greeting
  • "Hoe gaat het?" + response
  • At least one politeness word
  • A leave-taking expression

Length: 6-8 lines total

Task 7: Optional Challenge ​

Have a 1-minute greeting conversation (in person or via video) with a Dutch speaker or language partner. Practice:

  • Greeting appropriately
  • Asking how they are
  • Listening to their response
  • Thanking them
  • Saying goodbye

Summary ​

Congratulations! You've completed A0-04: Greeting and Basic Politeness.

Key Takeaways ​

You now know:

  • ✓ Time-of-day greetings (goedemorgen, goedemiddag, goedenavond) and when to use each
  • ✓ How to ask "How are you?" in both formal and informal Dutch (Hoe gaat het met u/je?)
  • ✓ Natural responses to greeting questions (Het gaat goed, Met mij gaat het goed, Prima, Heel goed)
  • ✓ Politeness formulas with formal/informal variants (dank je vs dank u, alsjeblieft vs alstublieft)
  • ✓ Multiple leave-taking expressions (tot ziens, doei, tot morgen, tot straks)
  • ✓ Simple imperative forms for polite requests (Zeg..., Vraag..., Doe...)
  • ✓ 40 new vocabulary words: greetings, leave-takings, politeness words, responses, structural words

What You Can Do Now ​

After this lesson, you can:

  • Greet people appropriately for morning, afternoon, and evening
  • Ask how someone is and understand common responses
  • Respond naturally to greeting questions
  • Choose formal or informal politeness words based on context
  • Say goodbye using context-appropriate leave-taking expressions
  • Conduct a complete 1-minute greeting exchange with a partner
  • Use simple imperative forms for polite requests

What Comes Next ​

The next lesson is A0-05: Counting and Basic Quantities. You'll learn:

  • Numbers 0-100 (beyond the 0-20 introduced in A0-02)
  • How to express quantities (a lot, a little, some, many, few)
  • Basic money vocabulary (euro, cent, price)
  • How to ask and answer questions about how many/how much

In that lesson, you'll practice real-world scenarios: "Hoeveel kost dit?" (How much does this cost?), "Ik heb tien euro" (I have ten euros), and "Veel plezier!" (Enjoy!).

Study Tips for Retention ​

  1. Practice greetings every morning in your target language. Make it a daily habit.
  2. Reread the Dialogue section 3 times. Familiar exchanges lock in natural phrasing.
  3. Record yourself greeting in Dutch and listen back. This builds confidence.
  4. Use greetings in real situations when possible. A language exchange partner or online community can help.
  5. Watch Dutch videos with focus on greetings and farewells. Notice stress, intonation, and context.
  6. Notice formality patterns. When native speakers use "u" vs "je," what's the context?
